A simple pattern: "For [customer] who [problem], we [what you do] so you can [result]." For example: "For busy pet owners who work late, we walk your dog at lunch so it gets exercise and you do not rush home." A clear offer is specific, honest and easy to repeat. It avoids vague phrases like "best quality" that do not say what the customer gets.
prompt: A founder wrote a clear offer but has no idea if customers care about the stated result. What should she check?
choices: A. Whether target customers say that result matters to them | B. Whether her family likes the wording | C. Whether the sentence has a nice rhythm when read aloud | D. Whether the font matches her logo
correct_answer: Whether target customers say that result matters to them
feedback: The offer's promised result must matter to the actual customers.
wrong_choices: B: family is not the target customer | C: style is secondary | D: not relevant to customer interest

section_skill: Plan interview questions about past behavior
outcome_title: Plan interview questions about what people already do rather than what they say they would do
intro: A customer interview is a short conversation to learn about someone's real problems. The most useful questions ask about what people already DID, not what they say they WOULD do. "Tell me about the last time you looked for a babysitter" gives real facts: how long it took, what they paid, what went wrong. "Would you use my babysitting app?" invites polite guesses. Past behavior is better evidence than predictions, because people are often too kind or too hopeful about the future.
prompt: Which interview question gives the most reliable information?
choices: A. Would you hire a tutor if I offered one next year? | B. Do you think tutoring is a good idea for most kids? | C. How much would you be willing to pay for my service? | D. When did you last hire a tutor, and how did you find one?
correct_answer: When did you last hire a tutor, and how did you find one?
feedback: Asking about a recent real event gives facts instead of guesses.
wrong_choices: A: it asks for a guess about the future | B: it asks for an opinion, not experience | C: it asks for a prediction about a product they have not seen

section_skill: Identify competitors and other alternatives
outcome_title: Identify direct competitors and the other ways customers solve the problem today
intro: Competitors are businesses selling something similar to the same customers. Alternatives are any other way customers solve the problem today, including doing it themselves, using a free tool, or doing nothing. A lawn-care business competes with other lawn services, but also with homeowners who mow their own lawns. Studying competitors and alternatives shows what customers already accept, what they pay, and what they complain about. "No competition" usually means you have not looked hard enough, or that few people want it.

feedback: Parents helping is another way to solve the problem, not a competing business.
wrong_choices: A: that is a direct competitor | C: that is a direct competitor | D: that is a direct competitor

outcome_title: Explain why likes, follows and compliments are weak demand signals
intro: Likes, follows, views and compliments feel good, but they are weak signs of demand. They cost people nothing, so many people give them freely. A post with 2,000 likes may lead to zero sales. Followers can also be people who enjoy your content but will never buy, or accounts that are not real people. feedback: Attention is not the same as buying.

intro: Limited liability has gaps. A PERSONAL GUARANTEE is a promise you sign to pay a business debt yourself if the business cannot. Lenders, landlords and some suppliers often ask new business owners for one, because the business has little history. If you sign it, your personal savings and other assets can be used to pay that debt, even if you have an LLC. Personal guarantees can be hidden in long forms. Read before signing, ask what you are guaranteeing, and consider whether the amount is one you could pay personally.

correct_answer: A promise to pay a business debt yourself if the business cannot
feedback: It makes you personally responsible for that debt.

section_skill: Explain what an EIN is and who usually needs one
outcome_title: Explain what an Employer Identification Number (EIN) is for and when to check whether one is needed
intro: An EIN (Employer Identification Number) is a nine-digit number the IRS (the federal tax agency) gives a business to identify it for federal taxes, much like a Social Security number identifies a person. Businesses that hire employees, most partnerships and corporations, and many LLCs need one. Banks often ask for it when opening a business account. Even a sole proprietor without employees may choose to get one so she can give clients the EIN instead of her Social Security number. The IRS says an EIN is free: you never have to pay a fee for one.

correct_answer: A federal tax ID number for a business
feedback: The IRS issues EINs to identify businesses for federal taxes.

intro: A separate business bank account keeps business money apart from personal money. All business income goes in and all business expenses come out of it. This makes bookkeeping and taxes easier, shows clearly what the business earns, and helps support the separation between an LLC or corporation and its owner. Mixing personal and business money in one account is called COMMINGLING. It makes records confusing and can weaken liability protection. The SBA lists opening a business bank account as a launch step.

choices: A. It removes the need for licenses | B. It always lowers the owner's taxes | C. It makes the LLC a trademark | D. It can weaken liability protection
correct_answer: It can weaken liability protection
feedback: Mixing funds blurs the line between owner and LLC.

outcome_title: Match business records against the bank statement and explain differences
intro: RECONCILING means comparing your own records with the bank statement to make sure they match. Each month, check every deposit and withdrawal. section_skill: Tell apart the registered agent, mailing and physical addresses
outcome_title: Tell a mailing address, a physical business address and a registered-agent address apart
intro: A business can have different addresses for different jobs. The REGISTERED AGENT ADDRESS is where official legal papers are delivered; states usually require a physical street address in the state. The MAILING ADDRESS is where ordinary letters and bills go; it may be a PO Box in many cases. The PHYSICAL (or principal) ADDRESS is where the business actually operates. Some addresses appear in public state records, so a home-based owner may prefer not to use her home for every one. Each state sets its own rules; Washington, for example, does not allow a PO Box as the registered agent address.
